city.caveat: This is the official city record as kept, without adjustments. It joins several observing sites over the years, and a move, a new instrument or the city growing around a station can shift readings (city growth mostly warms nights); NOAA's adjusted climate datasets correct for these. Treat any single number as approximate.

text.t_rec: Chicago has nearly stopped setting record lows
text.p_rec: If Chicago's climate weren't changing, every year would have the same chance of holding a daily record. Since 2000, Chicago has set 30 standing record lows, far fewer than the 63 that chance alone would give, and 74 record highs, close to the 63 that chance alone would give. The 1950s hold the most record highs of any decade (55). Chicago's all-time high is 105°F, on July 24, 1934.
text.t_chg: Chicago's nights have warmed since 1986. Its days warmed over the long run.
text.p_chg: Across 153 complete years: Chicago's average low shows no clear change: −0.04°F per decade, a range (−0.11 to +0.03) that includes zero. Chicago's average high has risen +0.32°F per decade (95% range +0.26 to +0.39), about +4.9°F since 1873. The last 40 years tell a different story: since 1986, lows have risen +1.08°F per decade (95% range +0.61 to +1.55) and highs show no clear change. The full record joins different observing sites over the years, and a move (for example, from the city to a cooler airport) can hide or exaggerate a long-run trend, so the recent decades are the clearer guide here.
text.t_mon: Lows rose in none; September and October fell. Highs rose in 9 of 12 months.
text.p_rain: Chicago's yearly precipitation has risen +0.37 inches per decade (95% range +0.15 to +0.58), about +5.6 inches since 1871. The 1991–2020 normal is 37.9 inches a year. The wettest year was 2008 (50.86 in); the driest, 1962 (22.22 in).
